title: The Red-Headed League
author: Arthur Conan Doyle
summary: Um homem de cabelo vermelho muito forte procura Sherlock Holmes com uma história estranha: ele foi pago para copiar um livro inteiro num escritório misterioso. Um dia, o escritório fecha sem explicação. Holmes e o Dr. Watson começam a investigar, e o caso curioso esconde algo muito maior em Londres.

chapters.title: A Man with Red Hair
paragraphs: It is autumn in London. I am visiting my friend, Sherlock Holmes. He is sitting in his chair at Baker Street. A big man is with him. The man is old and fat. His hair is very red, like fire.
“Come in, Watson,” says Holmes. “This is Mr. Jabez Wilson. He has a very strange story.”
Mr. Wilson looks at me. He is a little nervous. He takes a newspaper from his coat. “Look at this,” he says. “It is an advertisement.”
I read it. It says: “The Red-Headed League. A new job is open. The pay is four pounds a week. The work is easy. Only men with red hair can come. Come to Fleet Street on Monday at eleven.”
“Four pounds a week for easy work!” I say. “That is a lot of money.”
“Yes,” says Mr. Wilson. “I have a small shop. I lend money to people. Business is not good. So I need the money.”
Holmes smiles. “Tell us everything, Mr. Wilson. Start at the beginning.”

“Well,” says Mr. Wilson, “I have a young assistant. His name is Vincent Spaulding. He is clever, and he works for half pay. He likes photography. He goes down to the cellar every day with his camera. One day he shows me this newspaper. ‘You must go, Mr. Wilson,’ he says. ‘Your hair is perfect.’”

chapters.title: The Strange Job
paragraphs: “So I go to Fleet Street with Spaulding,” says Mr. Wilson. “There are hundreds of men there. Every man has red hair. Some have orange hair, some have brown hair. But my hair is the reddest of all.”
“We go into a small office. A little man is sitting at a table. His name is Duncan Ross. His hair is red too. He looks at my hair for a long time. Then he pulls it, very hard.”
“‘I am sorry,’ he says. ‘Some men wear wigs. I must be careful.’ Then he smiles. ‘The job is yours, Mr. Wilson!’”
Holmes listens with his eyes closed. “And what is the work?” he asks.

“It is very easy,” says Mr. Wilson. “I must sit in the office from ten to two every day. I must copy the Encyclopaedia Britannica with a pen. That is all. But I must not leave the office. If I leave, I lose the job.”
“And your shop?” asks Holmes.
“Spaulding takes care of the shop in the morning. Business is always quiet then. So I say yes.”

“Every day I go to the office. I write and write. I copy the words about Abbots, and Archery, and Armour. Every Saturday, Mr. Ross gives me four gold coins. I am very happy. This goes on for eight weeks.”
“And then?” I ask.
Mr. Wilson takes a small card from his pocket. “Then, this morning, the door is locked. There is this card on it.”
Holmes reads the card. It says: “The Red-Headed League is dissolved. October 9, 1890.”
Holmes and I look at the card. Then we look at Mr. Wilson's sad face. We laugh and laugh.
“It is not funny!” says Mr. Wilson. He is angry. “I want to know the truth. Who are these people?”

chapters.title: Holmes Thinks
paragraphs: “I am sorry, Mr. Wilson,” says Holmes. “Your case is very interesting. Please tell me about your assistant, Spaulding. What does he look like?”
“He is small and quick,” says Mr. Wilson. “He has no hair on his face. He is about thirty years old. And he has a white mark on his head. It is from acid.”
Holmes sits up in his chair. His eyes are bright. “Are his ears pierced, for earrings?”
“Yes!” says Mr. Wilson. “How do you know?”
“Thank you, Mr. Wilson,” says Holmes. “Today is Saturday. By Monday, I can help you. Good morning.”
Mr. Wilson goes home. Holmes sits in his chair with his long pipe. He does not speak for fifty minutes. Then he jumps up.
“Watson, come with me,” he says. “We are going to Mr. Wilson's street.”

We go to Saxe-Coburg Square. It is a small, poor square. Mr. Wilson's shop has three gold balls over the door. Holmes walks up and down. He looks at the houses. Then he hits the street hard with his stick, two or three times.
Next he knocks on the door of the shop. A young man opens it. He is quick and clever. Holmes asks him the way to the Strand. The young man tells him, and he closes the door.
“That is Spaulding,” says Holmes. “He is the fourth cleverest man in London. I know his face. And I want to see his knees.”
“His knees?” I ask. “Why?”

Holmes does not answer. We walk around the corner. Here is a big, busy street with rich shops. There is a restaurant, a newspaper office and a bank. The bank is the City and Suburban Bank. It is right behind Mr. Wilson's shop.
“Now I understand,” says Holmes quietly.

chapters.title: In the Dark
paragraphs: That night, at ten o'clock, I go to Baker Street again. I have my gun in my pocket. Two men are with Holmes. One is Mr. Jones, a police detective. The other is Mr. Merryweather. He is a director of the City and Suburban Bank.
“Tonight we are playing a game,” says Holmes. “The prize is thirty thousand pounds. And the player is John Clay.”
“John Clay!” says Mr. Jones. “He is a murderer and a thief. He is young, but he is very clever. Every policeman in London wants to catch him.”
We go to the bank in a cab. Mr. Merryweather opens a door. We walk down some stone steps. We are in a big cellar. There are many wooden boxes.
“There is French gold in these boxes,” says Mr. Merryweather. “Thirty thousand gold coins. It is a secret.”

“Not a secret from John Clay,” says Holmes. He takes his lamp and looks at the floor. Then he hits the stones with his stick. “Good. It is not hollow here. We must wait. Please, sit down and be quiet.”
Holmes covers the lamp. Now it is completely dark. We wait and wait. One hour goes by. Then another hour. I am cold and tired. My legs hurt. I hear only the breathing of the other men.
Then I see a small light. It is coming from the floor! A stone moves. A white hand comes up, then a face. It is a young face, with a mark on the head. It is Spaulding!
He climbs into the cellar. He turns and helps another man. This man has very red hair.

chapters.title: The Answer
paragraphs: “It's all clear,” says the young man. Then he sees us. “Jump, Archie, jump!” he shouts.

Holmes jumps at him and holds his coat. The red-haired man goes back down the hole. Mr. Jones runs after him, but he is too late. Spaulding takes out a gun. Holmes hits his hand with his stick. The gun falls on the floor.
“It's no use, John Clay,” says Holmes. “You have no chance.”
“I see that,” says Clay. He is very calm. “But my friend is free.”
“No,” says Holmes. “There are three policemen at the door of the shop.”
Mr. Jones puts handcuffs on Clay. “Please do not touch me with your dirty hands,” says Clay. “I have royal blood. Say ‘sir’ and ‘please’ to me.”
“All right,” says Jones with a smile. “Please, sir, walk up the steps.”
Later, Holmes and I are sitting at Baker Street. I ask him to explain everything.

“It is very simple, Watson,” he says. “The League is a trick. They want Wilson out of his shop for four hours every day. Why? His assistant works for half pay. And he goes down to the cellar every day. So he is digging. He is digging a tunnel. But to where?”
“To the bank!” I say.

“Yes. I hit the street with my stick. It is not hollow at the front. So the tunnel goes to the back. Behind the shop is the bank. And Spaulding's knees are dirty from digging. Then the League closes. So the tunnel is finished. They must use it soon. Saturday night is best, because the bank is closed on Sunday.”
“Holmes, you are wonderful,” I say.
He smiles and lights his pipe. “It saves me from a boring life, Watson. That is all.”
